title: Stock Market Indices Explained: S&P 500, Dow Jones, NASDAQ, and Russell 2000
content:
When you hear news anchors say 'the market was up today,' they're usually referring to one of several stock market indices. But what exactly is a stock market index, and what do these different indices actually track? Understanding the major indices is one of the most foundational skills for any investor.

## What Is a Stock Market Index?

A stock market index is a measurement tool that tracks the performance of a specific group of stocks. Think of it as a report card for a particular slice of the stock market. Instead of tracking every single stock, an index selects a representative sample and measures how those stocks perform collectively over time.

Indices serve several purposes: they give investors a quick snapshot of market health, they serve as benchmarks for portfolio performance, and they can be invested in directly through index funds or ETFs (Exchange-Traded Funds).

## The S&P 500: The Market's Benchmark

The Standard & Poor's 500 — universally known as the S&P 500 — is widely considered the most important stock market index in the world. It tracks 500 of the largest publicly traded companies in the United States, covering approximately 80% of the total US stock market's value.

The S&P 500 is a **market-capitalization-weighted** index, meaning companies with larger market values have a greater influence on the index's movement. As of recent years, the top five companies (often tech giants like Apple, Microsoft, Nvidia, Amazon, and Alphabet) can account for 20–25% of the index's total weight.

To be included in the S&P 500, a company must meet strict criteria: it must be a US company, have a market cap of at least $14.5 billion, be highly liquid, have at least 50% of its shares available for public trading, and have reported positive earnings in the most recent quarter plus positive cumulative earnings over the prior four quarters.

The S&P 500 is the standard benchmark most professional fund managers are compared against. When a fund manager says they 'beat the market,' they usually mean they outperformed the S&P 500.

## The Dow Jones Industrial Average: The Oldest and Most Famous

The Dow Jones Industrial Average (DJIA), often simply called 'the Dow,' was created in 1896 by Charles Dow and Edward Jones. It is the oldest major US stock index still in use today. Despite its fame, the Dow only tracks 30 large, well-established American companies — sometimes called 'blue chip' stocks.

The companies in the Dow are selected by editors at The Wall Street Journal rather than by a strict quantitative formula. Current members include household names like Apple, Boeing, Coca-Cola, Goldman Sachs, Johnson & Johnson, and Walmart.

Unlike the S&P 500, the Dow is **price-weighted**, meaning a company's stock price — not its total market value — determines its influence on the index. This is a quirky feature: a $500 stock from a mid-sized company will have more influence on the Dow than a $150 stock from a trillion-dollar company. This is widely considered a methodological weakness, and many analysts view the S&P 500 as a more accurate barometer of the overall market.

That said, the Dow remains culturally significant and is widely reported because of its long history and the prominence of its member companies.

## The NASDAQ Composite: Tech-Heavy and Growth-Oriented

The NASDAQ Composite tracks all stocks listed on the NASDAQ exchange — over 3,000 companies in total. Because the NASDAQ exchange has historically attracted technology and growth-oriented companies, the NASDAQ Composite is heavily weighted toward tech, biotech, and consumer internet companies.

Major components include Apple, Microsoft, Amazon, Alphabet (Google), Meta, Tesla, and Nvidia. Because of this tech concentration, the NASDAQ tends to be more volatile than the S&P 500 — it rises faster in bull markets and falls harder during downturns.

A related index, the **NASDAQ-100**, tracks only the 100 largest non-financial companies on the NASDAQ exchange and is the basis for the popular QQQ ETF. When investors talk about 'investing in NASDAQ,' they usually mean an ETF tracking the NASDAQ-100.

## The Russell 2000: The Small-Cap Benchmark

While the S&P 500 covers large companies, the Russell 2000 covers the 2,000 smallest companies in the Russell 3000 index (which itself covers the 3,000 largest US stocks). The Russell 2000 is the go-to benchmark for small-cap stocks — companies with market capitalizations generally between $300 million and $2 billion.

Small-cap stocks tend to be more domestically focused (less international revenue), more sensitive to the US economy, and have higher growth potential alongside higher risk. The Russell 2000 often diverges from the S&P 500 during periods of economic stress or when the US dollar is strong (since small caps earn more revenue domestically).

## How to Use Indices as an Investor

For most individual investors, the most practical use of these indices is as benchmarks and investment vehicles. Rather than trying to pick individual stocks, many people invest in low-cost index funds that simply replicate these indices. The Vanguard S&P 500 ETF (VOO), SPDR S&P 500 ETF (SPY), and iShares Russell 2000 ETF (IWM) are examples.

When evaluating your own portfolio, compare your returns to the most relevant index. If you invest primarily in large US companies, the S&P 500 is your benchmark. If you invest in small-cap stocks, compare yourself to the Russell 2000.

Understanding what each index measures helps you interpret financial news accurately and make more informed investment decisions.
